questions.question: A sentence/part will almost never begin with which of the following?
options: V2, V3, or the Objective Case (me, him, them)
Subject (Noun/Pronoun)
An article like 'A' or 'The'
A proper noun
questions.rationale: A part opening with a past-tense/participle verb form (V2/V3) or an objective-case pronoun (me, him, them) almost never starts a sequence — these depend on something already introduced.

questions.question: According to the pronoun-antecedent rule, when can a part beginning with 'he', 'she', or 'they' be the opening part?
options: Always — pronouns are neutral
Only if the pronoun is capitalized
Only if a noun it refers to has already appeared earlier — so it's very unlikely to be the opening part
Never, under any circumstance
questions.rationale: A pronoun must refer back to a noun that has already appeared — since nothing has appeared before the opening part, a part starting with a bare pronoun is very unlikely to be first.

questions.question: Words like 'however', 'therefore', and 'moreover' are strong clues that a part is:
options: The opening part
A middle or closing part, since they connect to something stated earlier
Irrelevant to sequencing
Always the second part specifically
questions.rationale: Transition/contrast words connect to an idea already introduced, so a part beginning with one of these is almost never the first part of the sequence.

questions.question: What does the definite article ('the') vs indefinite article ('a/an') clue typically indicate?
options: 'The' introduces a noun for the first time; 'a/an' refers back to it
'The' always marks the final sentence
Articles have no bearing on sequencing
'A/an' usually introduces a noun first; 'the' refers back to it once already known
questions.rationale: A noun is typically introduced with 'a/an' (indefinite) first, then referred to again with 'the' (definite) once it is already known to the reader — the indefinite mention usually comes first.

questions.question: In Practice Set 2 (A: 'Reading books regularly improves vocabulary and comprehension.' B: 'Therefore, students should be encouraged to read more.' C: 'It also helps develop critical thinking skills.' D: 'These benefits are especially important during school years.'), which part opens the sequence, and why?
options: A, because it introduces the general claim with no pronoun or article dependency
B, because it states a conclusion
D, because it lists benefits
C, because it uses 'it' referring back
questions.rationale: A introduces the general claim about reading with a full noun phrase and no pronoun dependency, making it the natural opening sentence; C's 'it' and B's 'Therefore' both depend on something stated earlier.

questions.question: According to the pronoun-antecedent rule, why is a part beginning with 'He discovered...' unlikely to be the opening sentence?
options: Because 'He' is grammatically incorrect
Because sentences can never start with pronouns
Because the pronoun 'He' must refer back to a noun introduced in an earlier part
Because 'discovered' is always a middle-sentence verb
questions.rationale: A pronoun like 'he' needs an antecedent — a noun it refers back to — that must already have appeared earlier in the sequence, so a part opening with it is very unlikely to be first.

questions.question: Which pair correctly illustrates the definite vs indefinite article clue?
options: 'The boy was standing near the gate' before 'A boy then walked inside'
'A boy was standing near the gate' before 'The boy then walked inside'
Both orders are equally valid
Articles provide no useful clue for sequencing
questions.rationale: A noun is typically introduced with the indefinite article ('a boy') and referred to again later with the definite article ('the boy'), once the reader already knows which boy is meant.

questions.question: Why is a part beginning with 'However, ...' almost never the first sentence in a sequence?
options: 'However' is grammatically incorrect at a sentence's start
Transition/contrast words like 'however' connect to an idea stated earlier, signalling a middle or closing part
'However' can only appear in questions
It has no bearing on sequencing
questions.rationale: Transition and contrast words such as however, but, moreover, and therefore connect back to something already stated, so a part opening with one of them is almost never the first part of the sequence.

questions.question: In Example 4 (frogs falling into a pit), what clue signals that part C ('When the other frogs saw how deep the pit was') comes after part A ('A group of frogs was travelling...')?
options: Part C uses the definite phrase 'the other frogs', referring back to the group introduced in A
Part C is alphabetically after A
Part C is longer than A
There is no clue connecting them
questions.rationale: Part A introduces 'a group of frogs' (indefinite); part C's 'the other frogs' uses the definite article, referring back to the group already introduced in A — a clear definite-article dependency.

questions.question: What is the recommended final check after arranging all the jumbled parts?
options: Submit immediately without re-checking
Re-read the fully assembled sentence or paragraph to confirm it reads naturally and makes complete grammatical and logical sense
Only check the first and last parts
Count the number of words in each part
questions.rationale: The lesson's common-mistakes section stresses re-reading the final assembled sequence once fully ordered, to confirm it reads naturally and makes full grammatical and logical sense from start to end.
